# Recommendations and Promotions for a B2B Wholesaler

<p style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace; font-size:.8rem; letter-spacing:.02em;">
Recommendations · PyTorch · SASRec · Implicit ALS · Segmentation · Imputation · Assortment optimization · Causal ML · PySpark · MLflow · Delta Lake · Databricks · Python · 38 tests
</p>
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The business question

A wholesaler that sells through an ordering platform serves thousands of small retailers. Each
week it has to decide what to put in front of each one: the products it reorders, the ones it
has never tried, the shelf a whole group of similar shops sees first, and which retailers get
a promotion that costs money. Part of the orders also arrive without an account number, and
those sales vanish from every customer history built on top of them.

This case answers the five questions on one public data set, with the same rule for all of
them: every model learns from the past and is scored on a period it never saw.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The data

[Online Retail II](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/502/online+retail+ii) (Chen, 2012, UCI
Machine Learning Repository, CC BY 4.0) holds every invoice line of a UK online seller of
gift-ware from 1 December 2009 to 9 December 2011: 1,067,371 lines, 39,516 sale invoices,
5,852 customers in about 40 countries and 4,707 products. The data set notes that many of its
customers are wholesalers, which makes it one of the few public B2B order logs.

It is also messy in the ways real order data is, and each problem is counted before anything
is modeled. 19,494 lines are cancellations; 34,335 are exact duplicates, 22,844 of them
because the two sheets of the workbook both contain 1 to 9 December 2010; 6,093 carry codes
that are not products (postage, bank charges, manual adjustments); 6,207 have a zero or
negative price; 7,881 have a price more than ten times above or below the usual price of the
same product, and are kept but flagged. After cleaning, 1,003,214 sale lines remain.

The largest gap is the customer: 22.6% of the sale lines, 13.1% of the revenue, have no
customer number.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Method, and why this one

**One cutoff for everything.** Models learn from the orders before 9 October 2011 and are
scored on the last 61 days. Their settings were chosen on the 61 days before that, so the test
window was used once. 12.5% of the revenue in the test window comes from products never sold
before the cutoff, which no model here can recommend.

**Two recommendation tasks, not one.** For a wholesaler, most of the next order repeats past
orders. Recommending "what you already buy" and "what you have never bought" are different
jobs, and they are scored separately. Five models compete: popularity in the last 90 days,
"buy again", item-to-item co-purchase, implicit ALS, and a sequential model in PyTorch that
reads each customer's orders in sequence with a GRU and scores every product for the next
order. Each recommendation shows the customer's own product it is most often bought with, so
a sales rep can explain it. Scores are Recall@10 and NDCG@10 with 95% bootstrap intervals over
customers.

**Segments that a manager can name.** Customers are grouped by recency, frequency, revenue,
basket size and range of products, with k-means and the number of groups chosen by
silhouette. The names come from the medians of each group.

**Imputation evaluated, not assumed.** To see whether orders without a customer number can be
attributed, the number is hidden on orders where it is known, and each basket is matched to
the purchase profiles of known customers in the same country.

**A shelf with variety.** For each segment, a mixed-integer program picks the 30 products with
the highest recent segment revenue with at most 4 from any product family (families come from
the product descriptions, since the data has no category). It is compared with the segment's
top sellers and the overall top sellers on what the segment bought in the test window.

**Promotions on a semi-synthetic experiment.** The data has no promotions, so a randomized
voucher is simulated on the real customers: each customer's spend without the voucher is the
real spend in the test window, and the voucher's effect is a known function of the
customer's real history (it brings back lapsed customers who used to spend, and gives away a
discount to frequent buyers who would have ordered anyway). Because the true effect is known
for every customer, any targeting rule can be scored exactly. This measures whether uplift
models find who responds; it does not show how this wholesaler's customers respond to real
promotions.

**Version 2: transformers.** SASRec, the self-attention recommender of Kang and McAuley
(2018), joins the comparison in two forms: read product by product, as published, and read
basket by basket, with each order as one step, the same way the GRU reads it. Both have their
number of epochs chosen on the validation window.

**Version 2: real campaigns.** The simulated voucher above says whether the methods can find who
responds; it cannot say how real customers respond. For that, the case adds a second public
panel with real campaigns: The Complete Journey, a year of purchases by 2,469 households of a
US grocery chain, with the households each campaign reached and the coupons they redeemed. The
three largest campaigns each reached about 1,100 households, but they were not randomized, so
every estimate is observational and checked against a placebo. The effect on weekly spend is
estimated with augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW), cross-fitted, adjusting for each
household's spend, trips, range of products, discounts, coupons and earlier campaigns. The
placebo runs the same estimator on the weeks just before the campaign, which the campaign cannot
have caused. A third estimate uses the change in spend, which removes selection on stable
spending levels. A doubly robust learner ranks households by their estimated effect, a best
linear predictor test (Chernozhukov et al.) checks whether that ranking captures real
differences, and every targeting rule is scored by its AIPW policy value. A 0-1 knapsack in
scipy picks households under a coupon budget.

**Version 2: lakehouse and tracking.** The pipeline writes bronze, silver and gold Delta tables
(raw lines, clean sales, customer features with segments, and the evaluation table), logs every
run to MLflow with the chosen settings and each model's metrics, and ships a Databricks Asset
Bundle that runs the same steps as a three-task job on Unity Catalog.

**Spark, with a parity test.** The cleaning rules and an implicit ALS are also written in
PySpark. CI runs them on a sample of the raw file and fails if Spark and pandas disagree on
any sale line.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Result

**Most of the next order is a reorder.** Scored on everything customers bought in the test
window, the simplest rule wins by far: offering each customer its own most frequent products
("buy again") reaches an NDCG@10 of 0.341, against 0.260 for the sequential model, the best of
the learned ones. A recommender that skips reorders leaves the easiest value of a B2B platform
on the table.

| Model, all products (2,041 customers) | Recall@10 | NDCG@10 (95% interval) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Buy again | 0.327 | 0.341 (0.329 to 0.353) |
| Sequential GRU (PyTorch) | 0.243 | 0.260 (0.249 to 0.271) |
| Implicit ALS | 0.195 | 0.196 (0.187 to 0.205) |
| Item-to-item (co-purchase) | 0.160 | 0.163 (0.154 to 0.172) |
| Popularity (last 90 days) | 0.100 | 0.102 (0.096 to 0.109) |

**For products the customer has never bought, the learned models earn their place.** The
sequential model (0.071) and implicit ALS (0.070) tie: the difference, 0.002, has an interval
from -0.004 to 0.007. Both beat co-purchase (0.059) and popularity (0.045). The numbers are low
because the task is hard: ten tries to find, among 4,529 products, the few a customer will buy
for the first time in the next two months.

| Model, products new to the customer (1,917 customers) | Recall@10 | NDCG@10 (95% interval) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sequential GRU (PyTorch) | 0.073 | 0.071 (0.066 to 0.077) |
| Implicit ALS | 0.071 | 0.070 (0.064 to 0.075) |
| Item-to-item (co-purchase) | 0.063 | 0.059 (0.054 to 0.065) |
| Popularity (last 90 days) | 0.048 | 0.045 (0.041 to 0.049) |

**Three segments, and one of them is the business.** Silhouette picked three groups. A third
of the customers, active (a median of 27 days since the last order and 9 orders), bring 83.5%
of the revenue before the cutoff. Almost half had not ordered for a median of 295 days.

| Segment | Customers | Share of revenue | Median days since last order | Median orders | Median revenue |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Top, active | 1,821 | 83.5% | 27 | 9 | £3,060 |
| Mid-value, lapsed | 2,543 | 12.9% | 295 | 2 | £560 |
| Low-value, lapsed | 1,108 | 3.5% | 312 | 1 | £201 |

**Orders without a customer number should not be attributed automatically.** With the number
hidden on the 4,790 orders of the test window, the basket matching puts the right customer
first 22.5% of the time and in the top ten 46.3% of the time, among customers seen before,
against 4.4% and 11.1% for the busiest customers of the same country. It narrows the search,
but even its most confident quarter of matches is right only 24.1% of the time, and 12.2% of
the orders come from customers never seen before. The orders without a number also look
different: the typical one has 20 lines against 15, at a typical unit price of £3.36 against
£1.97, which points to another sales channel rather than known accounts that did not log in.
The pipeline keeps them out of the customer histories and turns the matches into a review
queue: in the test window, 29 of the 227 orders without a number reach the confidence of the
top quarter.

**A shelf with variety holds up where it matters.** For the top segment, the optimized shelf
of 30 products covered 12.6% of what those customers bought in the test window and reached
76.8% of them, against 11.6% and 72.6% for the segment's top sellers and 11.9% and 72.3% for
the overall top sellers, with 12 product families instead of 7 and 9. In the two lapsed
segments the cap costs a little revenue coverage (8.1% against 8.5%, and 4.5% against 4.9%).
In every segment, the shelf that covers the most revenue is one built for that segment.

**Promotion targeting: the models pay off on small budgets.** In the simulated voucher test on
the 5,472 customers with history (10 replications), giving the voucher to the 20% of customers
the X-learner ranks highest brings £39,590 of true incremental revenue, against £21,940 for
random targeting, £23,488 for the top spenders and £23,892 for the most lapsed customers; an
oracle that knows every effect would reach £102,578. Learning who responds is hard because
spend varies by orders of magnitude between customers. Dividing the outcome by each customer's
past monthly revenue before fitting, which keeps the estimate unbiased under random
assignment, raised the X-learner's area under the gain curve from 13% to 23% of the oracle's.

Over the whole range of budgets, the rule "most lapsed first" still covers the most area, 45%
of the oracle's, because the simulated effect was built around lapsed customers and the rule
happens to match it. With an effect twice as large the X-learner reaches 41%; with four times
as large, the three learners on the scaled outcome pass the rule (the X-learner reaches 61%).
For a real campaign: a randomized test on about 5,500 customers already pays off when the
budget is small and targeted; ranking the whole base needs a larger effect or a larger test.
**Version 2: SASRec ties when it reads orders, and fails when it reads products.** On the same
test window:

| Model | New to the customer, NDCG@10 | All products, NDCG@10 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sequential GRU (PyTorch) | 0.071 (0.066 to 0.077) | 0.260 (0.249 to 0.271) |
| Implicit ALS | 0.070 (0.064 to 0.075) | 0.196 (0.187 to 0.205) |
| SASRec, basket by basket | 0.069 (0.063 to 0.074) | 0.251 (0.240 to 0.262) |
| SASRec, product by product | 0.017 (0.014 to 0.019) | 0.075 (0.069 to 0.081) |

Read product by product, as in the original paper, SASRec does worst of all: inside a wholesale
order the products have no order of their own, so "the next product" is mostly noise. Read order
by order, it lands with the GRU and ALS, within each other's intervals. A newer architecture does
not beat the recurrent model here; how the sequence is defined matters more than the encoder.

**Version 2: the real campaigns show selection, not effect.** Households that got a campaign
spent about US$ 34 to 37 a week more during it than those that did not. The placebo shows where
that gap comes from: they already spent as much more in the weeks before. After adjustment:

| Campaign | Raw difference | Adjusted, campaign weeks | Placebo, weeks before | Change in spend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 (May to June 2017) | +33.7 | +7.6 ± 7.2 | +5.2 ± 6.9 | +2.7 ± 5.2 |
| 13 (August to September) | +36.6 | +3.9 ± 12.6 | +0.3 ± 11.9 | +2.1 ± 7.3 |
| 18 (November to December) | +36.3 | -0.2 ± 9.3 | +1.0 ± 6.3 | -1.2 ± 5.7 |

US$ per household per week, with 95% intervals. No campaign has a detectable effect on spend,
and the smallest effect this design could detect on the change in spend is US$ 7.5 to 10.5 a
week, against a typical spend of about US$ 39. The doubly robust learner finds no heterogeneity
it can rank on: the best linear predictor slopes are 0.10, 0.00 and 0.15, none clearly above zero.
So the model-based targeting rule is no better than random here, and the case says so instead of
showing a gain curve. What the data does support is the next step: a randomized test, sized in
the app below, on the change in spend.

:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Limits

The data covers one seller of gift-ware in 2009 to 2011, mostly in the UK; the numbers are
evidence about the methods, not about any other company. The promotion experiment is
simulated on real customers, so it tests the targeting methods, not real price sensitivity.
Products launched in the test window cannot be recommended by any of these models; a
content-based model on product attributes would be the next step. The Spark job runs locally
in CI on a sample; it has not run on a cluster. The Databricks bundle has not been deployed to
a workspace: CI checks that it parses and that its tasks point to working scripts. The real
campaigns come from a US grocery chain, not a wholesaler, and were not randomized; the placebo
supports the adjustment for campaigns 13 and 18 better than for campaign 8.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Applied to your business

For a distributor, a wholesaler or a B2B ordering platform, the same pipeline runs on your
order history: suggested orders per customer, with the reason next to each item; segments
with a shelf per segment; a targeting rule for each promotion, tested before the budget is
spent; and a review queue for orders without an account. It starts with the
<a href="../oquant.html#packages">Data &amp; AI Diagnostic</a> and runs in your environment.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Code

```{=html}
<p>
<a class="rh-btn" href="https://github.com/rhozon/b2b-retail-recommender">github.com/rhozon/b2b-retail-recommender</a>
</p>
```

With Python 3.11 or later and the workbook in `~/data/online-retail-ii`:

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest -v
python -m b2bretail.cli --out results --lake lake --track sqlite:///mlflow.db
python -m b2bretail.promos --out results    # real campaigns, The Complete Journey
databricks bundle deploy -t dev             # with a Databricks workspace
```

The suite has **38 tests**. CI runs them on every push, and a second job with Java 17
runs the Spark parity tests and the Spark job.
:::
